## Appearance

Uncle Jim is a tall, rather ungainly figure who is somewhat stooped, yet his posture suggests great strength and endurance. He has a clean-shaven, deeply lined, and bronzed face, framed by a thick mane of hair falling to his shoulders that has grown increasingly gray. His remarkably blue, deep-set eyes are clear and steady, sometimes twinkling and sometimes dreaming. Though he appears very frail and bent at times, his steadfast spirit shines through his gaze.

_Sources: [v4 CHAPTER 6 CAPTAIN JIM P14](../source/v04-c06.md#nw-v04-c06-p0014), [v4 CHAPTER 30 LESLIE DECIDES P3](../source/v04-c30.md#nw-v04-c30-p0003), [v4 CHAPTER 30 LESLIE DECIDES P11](../source/v04-c30.md#nw-v04-c30-p0011)_

## Personality

Uncle Jim, also known as Captain Jim, is a high-souled, simple-minded man possessing a rare and fine soul with eternal youth in his eyes and heart. He maintains an invariable cheerfulness and placid demeanor, having formed a habit of enjoying things that prevents him from becoming angry. Passionate about worshipping beauty, he also enjoys philosophically pondering all kinds of problems despite not being able to solve them. He is a born storyteller with a talent for bringing far-off things vividly to life, and he possesses a tolerable skill at playing the fiddle. His primary fear is the horror of a lingering death.

_Sources: [v4 CHAPTER 6 CAPTAIN JIM P14](../source/v04-c06.md#nw-v04-c06-p0014), [v4 CHAPTER 8 MISS CORNELIA BRYANT COMES TO CALL P61](../source/v04-c08.md#nw-v04-c08-p0061), [v4 CHAPTER 9 AN EVENING AT FOUR WINDS POINT P5](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0005), [v4 CHAPTER 9 AN EVENING AT FOUR WINDS POINT P49](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0049), [v4 CHAPTER 14 NOVEMBER DAYS P3](../source/v04-c14.md#nw-v04-c14-p0003), [v4 CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT P6](../source/v04-c16.md#nw-v04-c16-p0006), +4 more_

## History

Born into a family of sea-going people, Uncle Jim ran off to sea as a boy and spent most of his life sailing the world. Over fifty years ago, he lost his sweetheart [Margaret](../character/margaret.md) when she drifted away in a dory, and he searched for her body along the shore for months. Throughout his adventurous travels, he gathered stories and material, eventually settling down at [Four Winds Harbor](../codex/places.md#four-winds-harbor) to tend the lighthouse five years prior to meeting [Anne](../character/anne.md) and [Gilbert Blythe](../character/gilbert-blythe.md). Recognizing [Anne](../character/anne.md) as a kindred spirit, he welcomed the couple into his life, sharing his collection of curios, entertaining them with sea tales, and introducing them to his orange cat, [First Mate](../character/first-mate.md). In time, he entrusted his cherished journal of sea adventures to [Anne](../character/anne.md) and [Gilbert](../character/gilbert-blythe.md), hoping his life story might one day be written down. Following the tragic loss of Anne's first child, he offered her comfort by sharing the history of his lost love [Margaret](../character/margaret.md) and asking [Anne](../character/anne.md) to keep her memory alive. When writer [Owen Ford](../character/owen-ford.md) visited [Four Winds](../codex/places.md#four-winds), Uncle Jim allowed him to borrow his life-book and collaborate on a manuscript weaving his sea experiences with Margaret's story. Later, Uncle Jim financially assisted [Leslie Moore](../character/leslie-moore.md) when she needed to travel to [Montreal](../codex/places.md#montreal), and he was honored when [Anne](../character/anne.md) and [Gilbert](../character/gilbert-blythe.md) named their newborn son [James Matthew](../character/james-a.md) after him. Aware of his impending death, he entrusted the care of [First Mate](../character/first-mate.md) to [Anne](../character/anne.md) shortly before bestowing a warm benediction upon [Leslie](../character/leslie-moore.md) and Owen when they announced their love. Upon receiving a published copy of his completed life-book from [Anne](../character/anne.md) and [Leslie](../character/leslie-moore.md), Uncle Jim peacefully passed away in his sleep at the lighthouse with the book resting on his chest.

_Sources: [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P1](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0001), [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P2](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0002), [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P5](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0005), [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P6](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0006), [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P7](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0007), [v2 II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure P14](../source/v02-c02.md#nw-v02-c02-p0014), +669 more_

## Quotes

> "The Government don’t give lighthouse keepers such luxuries. Look at the colors that wood makes. If you’d like some driftwood for your fire, Mistress Blythe, I’ll bring you up a load some day. Sit down. I’m going to make you a cup of tea."
>
> — Uncle Jim — [v4 CHAPTER 9 AN EVENING AT FOUR WINDS POINT P24](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0024)

> "That’s Marshall Elliott—a mighty fine man with jest one streak of foolishness in him. I s’pose you wondered what his object was in turning himself into a sort of dime museum freak."
>
> — Uncle Jim — [v4 CHAPTER 9 AN EVENING AT FOUR WINDS POINT P32](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0032)

> "Come, now, Cornelia, I can’t see any harm in going to the Methodist church when there’s no preaching in your own. I’ve been a Presbyterian for seventy-six years, and it isn’t likely my theology will hoist anchor at this late day."
>
> — Uncle Jim — [v4 CHAPTER 15 CHRISTMAS AT FOUR WINDS P23](../source/v04-c15.md#nw-v04-c15-p0023)

> "I wanted to hear some good singing. The Methodists have a good choir; and you can’t deny, Cornelia, that the singing in our church is awful since the split in the choir."
>
> — Uncle Jim — [v4 CHAPTER 15 CHRISTMAS AT FOUR WINDS P25](../source/v04-c15.md#nw-v04-c15-p0025)

> "That’s just exactly the truth about Lewis Taylor. When I see those poor, miserable children of his, robbed of all children ought to have, it p’isens my own bite and sup for days afterwards."
>
> — Uncle Jim — [v4 CHAPTER 15 CHRISTMAS AT FOUR WINDS P47](../source/v04-c15.md#nw-v04-c15-p0047)
